summary.html: AI products got more concrete: the clearest upgrades were about turning prompts into finished deliverables and better execution loops, not just bragging about raw model intelligence.
Infra was the real battleground: compute access, rate limits, and network efficiency kept showing up as the practical constraints shaping who can actually ship usable AI products.
The market read-through was more cautious than euphoric: several strong posts argued that value may accrue more to compute providers and overlooked breadth than to headline-chasing model hype.

Trust and control were recurring themes: from OpenAI governance drama to agent-memory design, the interesting question was less "what can the model do?" and more "who controls the system, and can you inspect it?"

items.title: @GeminiApp: Native Office File Exports
items.body: Gemini can now generate downloadable PDFs plus Google Workspace and Microsoft Office files directly from chat prompts. The practical shift is from "generate text" to "ship a usable deliverable" without a manual export step.

items.title: @RichNwan: Managed Agents Still Need Open Harnesses
items.body: A thoughtful agent-platform critique argued Anthropic's new Dreaming memory and Outcomes rubrics are useful, but closed managed-agent layers still leave teams blind on critical controls like PII filtering and memory policy. The takeaway is that open harnesses may stay strategically important even as labs add higher-level agent features.

items.title: @Xuegaogx: OpenAI's MRC Network Protocol
items.body: A detailed infra thread highlighted OpenAI's newly open MRC protocol for large training clusters, describing a design that cuts network layers and keeps jobs alive through switch failures. If the implementation holds up, training efficiency rather than just raw GPU count becomes a more meaningful competitive lever.

items.title: @vikingmute: A Self-Auditing Codex Prompt Loop
items.body: One widely shared Codex workflow asks the model whether it is truly 100% confident, then forces it to keep finding flaws and patching them until confidence is earned. It's a good pattern for getting stronger verification behavior from coding agents instead of accepting the first plausible answer.

items.title: @dotey: Debug Codex Desktop with Chrome DevTools
items.body: A handy workflow tip showed how to launch the Codex desktop app with a remote debugging port and inspect it through Chrome DevTools. That gives power users a practical way to study the app, trace behavior, and debug agent-assisted UI work.

items.title: @GaryMarcus: Murati Testimony Reframes Sam's Ouster
items.body: Gary Marcus argued the new Mira Murati testimony makes the 2023 Altman firing look less like an AI-safety rupture and more like a trust and governance breakdown. That matters because the court fight is turning internal OpenAI management questions into material industry news again.

items.title: @burkov: Compute Landlords May Be the Real Winners
items.body: Burkov's read on Elon renting GPU capacity to Anthropic was blunt: if even a rival lab is monetizing spare compute, the best business may be supplying infrastructure rather than trying to catch the model leader. It's a sharp reminder that AI economics may reward landlords and capacity brokers more than late model challengers.

items.title: @xiaochuan8688: S&P Highs Are Hiding Weak Breadth
items.body: A market thread argued that headline index highs are masking weakness across much of the S&P 500, with megacaps doing most of the lifting while many individual stocks lag. Even if you discount the exact numbers, the useful read-through is to separate headline index strength from actual market breadth before chasing momentum.

items.title: @op7418: Markdown Won the AI File-Format War
items.body: This post made a convincing case that Markdown has become the default shared substrate for AI memory, notes, and file exchange, with HTML handling richer presentation. The interesting implication is that the next product layer may be better interfaces on top of Markdown rather than yet another editor.

items.title: @pandemona: Searchable Podcast Data for Agents
items.body: Particle launched an API aimed at turning podcasts into queryable structured data, including mentions, clips, and metadata. If you rely on podcasts for research or market color, this felt like one of the more genuinely useful data-unlocking tools in the feed.

items.title: @tomhacks: Scarcity Is Easier to Forgive Than Spin
items.body: A blunt product-management critique argued that users will tolerate rate limits and compute shortages far better than confusing plan changes or quiet degradations. It was a good reminder that transparent bad news usually damages trust less than polished evasiveness.
